title: LLM Mechanics: Tokens, Context, and Cost
description: A practical quiz about how LLM APIs handle tokens, context, sampling, caching, streaming, structured output, and knowledge cutoffs. It includes production scenarios and cost calculations.

questions.title: What does a text LLM receive after tokenization?

images.alt: Four panels on tokenization. The first counts the string “Ada Lovelace!” three ways — 13 characters, 2 words, and the four tokenizer pieces "Ada", " Lov", "elace" and "!" — marking the token count as the one that is billed. The second shows three edits that move a boundary: a leading space turning "cat" into " cat", capitalization turning "cat" into "Cat", and a rare word turning "token" into "tokeniser". The third splits “strawberry” into st, raw and berry, noting the model never receives a list of letters. The fourth is a ladder from one grapheme to three code points, eleven UTF-8 bytes, and several tokens.
images.caption: Characters, words, graphemes, code points, bytes and tokens are six different units.

options.text: A sequence of token IDs produced by a tokenizer
One floating-point number for each sentence
A parse tree whose nodes are always English words
Raw Unicode characters with no preprocessing

questions.explanation: A tokenizer turns text into token IDs before the model processes it. A token may represent a common word, part of a word, punctuation, or a byte-based piece. That is why counting words or characters does not give an exact token count.
questions.references: [Hugging Face Transformers: Tokenization algorithms](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/tokenizer_summary)

options.text: It usually processes subword or byte-based tokens, so exact letter counting is an indirect task
The letter `r` is removed from all tokenizer vocabularies
Transformers cannot represent repeated symbols under any circumstances
The model sees only the word's dictionary definition

questions.explanation: The model may receive a whole word or a few fragments instead of a neat list of letters. It then has to reconstruct the spelling while predicting tokens, which makes exact counting harder. Spelling out the word or using a counting tool can make the result reliable.

options.text: A leading space can change the token ID used for the same visible word
Capitalization can change tokenization or token IDs
A rare word can split into several subword tokens
Every Unicode code point is guaranteed to map to exactly one token in every tokenizer

questions.explanation: A tokenizer uses pieces from its own vocabulary, not a universal one-character-per-token rule. Spaces and capitalization can change which vocabulary entry matches. Common text may stay in larger pieces, while rare text may split into smaller ones.
questions.references: [Hugging Face Transformers: Subword tokenization](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/tokenizer_summary)

questions.title: Why are subword tokenizers useful?

images.alt: Four panels on tokenization. The first counts the string “Ada Lovelace!” three ways — 13 characters, 2 words, and the four tokenizer pieces "Ada", " Lov", "elace" and "!" — marking the token count as the one that is billed. The second shows three edits that move a boundary: a leading space turning "cat" into " cat", capitalization turning "cat" into "Cat", and a rare word turning "token" into "tokeniser". The third splits “strawberry” into st, raw and berry, noting the model never receives a list of letters. The fourth is a ladder from one grapheme to three code points, eleven UTF-8 bytes, and several tokens.
images.caption: Characters, words, graphemes, code points, bytes and tokens are six different units.

options.text: Frequent words or fragments can remain compact
Unseen or rare words can be assembled from smaller known pieces
The vocabulary can stay smaller than a vocabulary containing every possible full word
All languages are guaranteed to use the same number of tokens for equivalent sentences

questions.explanation: Subword tokenization balances vocabulary size with the ability to represent unfamiliar text. Common words or fragments can stay compact, while rare words can be built from smaller pieces. Efficiency still depends on the tokenizer's training data, so equivalent sentences in different languages may use different numbers of tokens.
questions.references: [Hugging Face Transformers: Tokenization algorithms and tradeoffs](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/tokenizer_summary)

options.text: Use that model's tokenizer or the provider's token-counting endpoint, including message and tool overhead
Count spaces and add one
Multiply the number of English words by exactly 0.75
Use the character count because every character is one token

questions.explanation: Rules such as "one token is about four English characters" are only rough estimates. Exact counts depend on the model's encoding and can include messages, tools, images, files, and formatting. When cost or limits matter, count the complete request with model-aware tooling.

options.text: Yes. Visible graphemes, Unicode code points, bytes, and model tokens are different units
No. Every rendered glyph is exactly one token by definition
Only if the emoji appears at the start of a sentence
Only character-level tokenizers can encode emoji

questions.title: What is the difference between a context window and a maximum output limit?

images.alt: Three panels on a request's budget. The first draws one bar of what occupies a request — system and developer instructions, conversation history, tool definitions and results, a thin slice for the user's visible message, and images and files. The second shows a 128,000-token combined window filled to 119,500 with 8,500 left, next to a separate 16,000-token output cap, and the arithmetic 128,000 − 119,500 = 8,500 and min(16,000, 8,500) = 8,500. The third pairs a truncated conversation, where the earliest turns holding the rules and the uploaded spec are dropped while recent chatter is kept, with the three outcomes of a 2,000-token output cap: stopping early, cutting off mid-sentence, and never being a request for exactly 2,000.
images.caption: The output cap and the combined window are separate limits; the smaller one binds.

options.text: The context window bounds the tokens available to a request, while the output limit separately caps how many tokens may be generated
They are two names for the exact same number on every model
The context window counts characters, while the output limit counts words
The output limit controls only network packet size

questions.explanation: Providers list these limits separately because a model may accept far more context than it can generate in one response. The output limit caps generation. If the context window covers both input and output, the remaining context space can impose a lower cap.
questions.references: [OpenAI API: Model catalog with separate context-window and max-output fields](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models)

questions.title: What is the largest possible output in this request?
questions.description: A hypothetical API states `input tokens + output tokens ≤ 128,000` and also has a `16,000`-token maximum output. The complete input uses `119,500` tokens. Enter the number of output tokens.

images.alt: Three panels on a request's budget. The first draws one bar of what occupies a request — system and developer instructions, conversation history, tool definitions and results, a thin slice for the user's visible message, and images and files. The second shows a 128,000-token combined window filled to 119,500 with 8,500 left, next to a separate 16,000-token output cap, and the arithmetic 128,000 − 119,500 = 8,500 and min(16,000, 8,500) = 8,500. The third pairs a truncated conversation, where the earliest turns holding the rules and the uploaded spec are dropped while recent chatter is kept, with the three outcomes of a 2,000-token output cap: stopping early, cutting off mid-sentence, and never being a request for exactly 2,000.
images.caption: The output cap and the combined window are separate limits; the smaller one binds.

questions.explanation: The remaining context capacity is `128,000 - 119,500 = 8,500` tokens. The effective output ceiling is `min(16,000, 8,500) = 8,500`. The separate 16,000-token output cap cannot create more room in the combined budget.
questions.references: [OpenAI API: Models expose context and maximum-output limits separately](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models)

questions.title: What can happen when an API request sets a maximum output of 2,000 tokens?

images.alt: Three panels on a request's budget. The first draws one bar of what occupies a request — system and developer instructions, conversation history, tool definitions and results, a thin slice for the user's visible message, and images and files. The second shows a 128,000-token combined window filled to 119,500 with 8,500 left, next to a separate 16,000-token output cap, and the arithmetic 128,000 − 119,500 = 8,500 and min(16,000, 8,500) = 8,500. The third pairs a truncated conversation, where the earliest turns holding the rules and the uploaded spec are dropped while recent chatter is kept, with the three outcomes of a 2,000-token output cap: stopping early, cutting off mid-sentence, and never being a request for exactly 2,000.
images.caption: The output cap and the combined window are separate limits; the smaller one binds.

options.text: The model can stop before 2,000 tokens when it completes the answer or emits a stop condition
Generation can be cut off at the limit, leaving an incomplete answer
The setting is a ceiling, not a request to produce exactly 2,000 tokens
The setting guarantees a semantically complete answer of exactly 2,000 tokens

questions.explanation: A maximum-output setting is a ceiling, not a target. The model can stop earlier, or it can reach the limit and leave the answer incomplete. Applications should inspect the completion status before treating a response as complete.
questions.references: [OpenAI API: Structured Outputs edge cases include max-token truncation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs)

questions.title: Does fitting a document inside the context window guarantee that every detail will be used reliably?

images.alt: Three panels on a request's budget. The first draws one bar of what occupies a request — system and developer instructions, conversation history, tool definitions and results, a thin slice for the user's visible message, and images and files. The second shows a 128,000-token combined window filled to 119,500 with 8,500 left, next to a separate 16,000-token output cap, and the arithmetic 128,000 − 119,500 = 8,500 and min(16,000, 8,500) = 8,500. The third pairs a truncated conversation, where the earliest turns holding the rules and the uploaded spec are dropped while recent chatter is kept, with the three outcomes of a 2,000-token output cap: stopping early, cutting off mid-sentence, and never being a request for exactly 2,000.
images.caption: The output cap and the combined window are separate limits; the smaller one binds.

options.text: No. Capacity only means the tokens can be supplied; use of details can still depend on relevance and position
Yes. Attention guarantees lossless recall of every supplied token
Yes, but only when temperature is above 1
No, because models can read only the final 512 tokens of any context

questions.explanation: A context window tells you how much input fits, not how reliably every detail will be used. In the *Lost in the Middle* experiments, performance often fell when relevant information appeared in the middle of long inputs. Long-context systems still need careful retrieval, ordering, and evaluation.
questions.references: [Liu et al.: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)

questions.title: Which data can use a request's context budget?

images.alt: Three panels on a request's budget. The first draws one bar of what occupies a request — system and developer instructions, conversation history, tool definitions and results, a thin slice for the user's visible message, and images and files. The second shows a 128,000-token combined window filled to 119,500 with 8,500 left, next to a separate 16,000-token output cap, and the arithmetic 128,000 − 119,500 = 8,500 and min(16,000, 8,500) = 8,500. The third pairs a truncated conversation, where the earliest turns holding the rules and the uploaded spec are dropped while recent chatter is kept, with the three outcomes of a 2,000-token output cap: stopping early, cutting off mid-sentence, and never being a request for exactly 2,000.
images.caption: The output cap and the combined window are separate limits; the smaller one binds.

options.text: System, developer, and user instructions included in the request
Conversation history supplied or carried into the request
Tool definitions and tool results supplied to the model
Only the latest visible user sentence; all other request data uses no context

questions.explanation: The latest user message is only one part of a request. Instructions, conversation history, tool definitions, tool results, and multimodal inputs can all use tokens or equivalent units. This is why a short visible message can belong to a large model input.

questions.title: What is the main risk of removing the oldest items from an overlong conversation?

images.alt: Three panels on a request's budget. The first draws one bar of what occupies a request — system and developer instructions, conversation history, tool definitions and results, a thin slice for the user's visible message, and images and files. The second shows a 128,000-token combined window filled to 119,500 with 8,500 left, next to a separate 16,000-token output cap, and the arithmetic 128,000 − 119,500 = 8,500 and min(16,000, 8,500) = 8,500. options.text: Foundational instructions or facts may disappear while the request still appears to succeed
The tokenizer permanently deletes those messages from the user's database
The model automatically retrains itself on the omitted messages
Output tokens become free after truncation

questions.explanation: Removing old items changes the information available to the model. If those items contain important instructions or evidence, the model's behavior may change even though the request succeeds. Applications should manage or summarize long histories deliberately.

questions.title: What does an autoregressive text model repeatedly do during ordinary generation?

images.alt: Three panels on decoding. The first draws the generation loop as four steps — the context so far, a distribution over the whole vocabulary, sampling one token, appending it and running the step again. The second puts two bar charts side by side over the same five candidates: at T = 1.0 the probabilities read 0.45, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10 and 0.05, and at T = 0.2 they read 0.88, 0.09, 0.02, 0.01 and 0.00. The third works through top_p = 0.70 over sorted probabilities 0.45, 0.30, 0.15 and 0.10: the first two are kept, reaching a cumulative 0.75, and a dashed cut drops the rest.
images.caption: Nucleus sampling keeps whole candidates, so the retained mass can exceed top_p.

options.text: Compute a distribution for the next token, select one, append it, and repeat
Retrieve a completed answer verbatim from a database for every prompt
Generate all future tokens independently with no dependence on earlier output
Convert the prompt into a single immutable sentence template

questions.explanation: An autoregressive model predicts one token from the tokens that came before it. The selected token is appended to the sequence and affects the next prediction. A small difference early in generation can lead to a very different answer.
questions.references:
[Brown et al.: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165)

[Hugging Face Transformers: Text generation strategies](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/generation_strategies)

questions.title: What does lowering sampling temperature usually do to the next-token distribution?

images.alt: Three panels on decoding. The first draws the generation loop as four steps — the context so far, a distribution over the whole vocabulary, sampling one token, appending it and running the step again. The second puts two bar charts side by side over the same five candidates: at T = 1.0 the probabilities read 0.45, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10 and 0.05, and at T = 0.2 they read 0.88, 0.09, 0.02, 0.01 and 0.00. The third works through top_p = 0.70 over sorted probabilities 0.45, 0.30, 0.15 and 0.10: the first two are kept, reaching a cumulative 0.75, and a dashed cut drops the rest.
images.caption: Nucleus sampling keeps whole candidates, so the retained mass can exceed top_p.

options.text: It sharpens the distribution, favoring already-likely tokens more strongly
It makes every vocabulary token equally likely
It expands the model's knowledge cutoff
It increases the context window

questions.explanation: Temperature rescales the values used to compute sampling probabilities. A value below 1 widens the gaps, so already likely tokens receive more probability. This changes sampling behavior, not the model's knowledge or context window.
questions.references:
[Hugging Face Transformers: Generation parameters](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main_classes/text_generation)

[OpenAI API reference: Temperature controls randomness](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/responses/methods/create)

questions.title: What does `top_p: 0.9` mean in nucleus sampling?

images.alt: Three panels on decoding. The first draws the generation loop as four steps — the context so far, a distribution over the whole vocabulary, sampling one token, appending it and running the step again. The second puts two bar charts side by side over the same five candidates: at T = 1.0 the probabilities read 0.45, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10 and 0.05, and at T = 0.2 they read 0.88, 0.09, 0.02, 0.01 and 0.00. The third works through top_p = 0.70 over sorted probabilities 0.45, 0.30, 0.15 and 0.10: the first two are kept, reaching a cumulative 0.75, and a dashed cut drops the rest.
images.caption: Nucleus sampling keeps whole candidates, so the retained mass can exceed top_p.

options.text: Keep the smallest set of most-probable next tokens whose cumulative probability reaches at least 0.9, then sample from it
Keep exactly 90% of the vocabulary by token count
Always choose the token whose individual probability is exactly 0.9
Discard the most probable 10% of tokens

questions.explanation: Nucleus sampling uses cumulative probability, not a fixed percentage of the vocabulary. A confident prediction may need only a few candidates to reach 0.9. A flatter distribution may need many more.
questions.references:
[Holtzman et al.: The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.09751)

[Hugging Face Transformers: `top_p` generation parameter](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main_classes/text_generation)

questions.title: How many candidates are retained by this top-p filter?
questions.description: The sorted next-token probabilities are `[0.45, 0.30, 0.15, 0.10]`, and `top_p` is `0.70`. Retain the smallest prefix whose cumulative mass is at least `0.70`. Enter an integer.

images.alt: Three panels on decoding. The first draws the generation loop as four steps — the context so far, a distribution over the whole vocabulary, sampling one token, appending it and running the step again. The second puts two bar charts side by side over the same five candidates: at T = 1.0 the probabilities read 0.45, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10 and 0.05, and at T = 0.2 they read 0.88, 0.09, 0.02, 0.01 and 0.00. The third works through top_p = 0.70 over sorted probabilities 0.45, 0.30, 0.15 and 0.10: the first two are kept, reaching a cumulative 0.75, and a dashed cut drops the rest.
images.caption: Nucleus sampling keeps whole candidates, so the retained mass can exceed top_p.

questions.explanation: The first candidate contributes `0.45`, which is below `0.70`. Adding the second gives `0.45 + 0.30 = 0.75`, so the threshold has been reached with 2 candidates. The total can exceed `top_p` because the filter keeps whole candidates.
questions.references: [Holtzman et al.: Nucleus sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.09751)

questions.title: Why can the same visible prompt produce different answers?

options.text: Random sampling among plausible next tokens
A moving model alias or changed backend configuration
Different instructions, conversation history, tools, or request parameters
A mathematical law requiring every repeated prompt to produce byte-identical text

questions.explanation: Sampling can vary, but the visible prompt is not always the full request. Model version, instructions, earlier turns, tool results, and decoding settings can also differ. To investigate a change, record the complete request and the exact model version.
questions.references:
[OpenAI API: Model-version behavior can vary](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/overview#backwards-compatibility)

[Hugging Face Transformers: Text generation strategies](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/generation_strategies)

questions.title: When a model supports temperature 0, does that make its answer factually correct?

images.alt: Three panels on decoding. The first draws the generation loop as four steps — the context so far, a distribution over the whole vocabulary, sampling one token, appending it and running the step again. The second puts two bar charts side by side over the same five candidates: at T = 1.0 the probabilities read 0.45, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10 and 0.05, and at T = 0.2 they read 0.88, 0.09, 0.02, 0.01 and 0.00. The third works through top_p = 0.70 over sorted probabilities 0.45, 0.30, 0.15 and 0.10: the first two are kept, reaching a cumulative 0.75, and a dashed cut drops the rest.
images.caption: Nucleus sampling keeps whole candidates, so the retained mass can exceed top_p.

options.text: No. It can reduce sampling variation, but the preferred continuation can still be wrong
Yes. Zero temperature activates a fact database
Yes. Zero temperature moves the knowledge cutoff to the current date
No. Zero temperature always selects a uniformly random token

questions.explanation: Temperature changes how a model selects among possible continuations. A low setting can make answers more repeatable, but the most likely continuation can still contain a mistake. Factual claims still need evidence and validation.
questions.references: [Hugging Face Transformers: Temperature controls next-token sampling](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main_classes/text_generation)

questions.title: Which practices help reproduce or diagnose changes across repeated API runs?

options.text: Keep the model snapshot, request parameters, input, and seed fixed when the API supports a seed
Record the backend or system fingerprint when the provider exposes one
Pin a model snapshot instead of relying on an alias that can move
Assume a seed guarantees correctness and byte-identical output forever

questions.explanation: Some APIs offer a seed as a best-effort reproducibility control, not a permanent guarantee. Keeping the full request and model snapshot fixed removes other common sources of variation. Record any backend fingerprint the provider exposes, and use evals to catch changes.
questions.references:
[OpenAI API: Seed is a best-effort reproducibility control](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/chat)

questions.title: Why might an API recommend tuning either temperature or top-p rather than both at once?

images.alt: Three panels on decoding. The first draws the generation loop as four steps — the context so far, a distribution over the whole vocabulary, sampling one token, appending it and running the step again. The second puts two bar charts side by side over the same five candidates: at T = 1.0 the probabilities read 0.45, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10 and 0.05, and at T = 0.2 they read 0.88, 0.09, 0.02, 0.01 and 0.00. The third works through top_p = 0.70 over sorted probabilities 0.45, 0.30, 0.15 and 0.10: the first two are kept, reaching a cumulative 0.75, and a dashed cut drops the rest.
images.caption: Nucleus sampling keeps whole candidates, so the retained mass can exceed top_p.

options.text: Both reshape the candidate distribution, so changing both makes the effect harder to reason about and evaluate
The two parameters are aliases and always have identical numeric ranges
Using either parameter disables tokenization
Top-p controls only price, while temperature controls only latency

questions.explanation: Temperature reshapes the probability distribution, while top-p limits sampling to a cumulative-probability set. Changing both at once makes it harder to tell which setting caused an effect. Holding one steady makes experiments easier to interpret.

questions.title: Which prompt layout is most likely to maximize prefix-cache reuse across many requests?

images.alt: Three panels on prompt caching. The first compares two prompt layouts: a cache-hostile one that opens with a request id, so the prefix diverges at the first token, and a cache-friendly one that opens with stable instructions and examples and leaves 410 tokens of shared prefix before the request id and user data. The second lists what a hit is — a byte-identical opening, reported in the usage data, cheaper and faster on eligible input — against what it is not: a semantic match, free output, or learning; with a note that automatic caching starts at 1,024 prompt tokens. The third bills ten requests: one uncached at $0.020, nine cached at $0.018, and ten outputs at $0.080, totalling $0.118.
images.caption: A prefix match stops at the first changed token, so where the edit lands decides how much is reused.

options.text: Stable instructions and examples first, followed by request-specific data near the end
A changing timestamp first, followed by stable instructions
Randomize the order of tool definitions on every call
Insert a unique request ID at the beginning of every prompt

questions.explanation: Prompt caching matches the beginning of a request. Put shared instructions and examples first, then add variable user data. A changing timestamp or request ID near the start makes the requests diverge early and reduces cache reuse.

questions.title: At what prompt length is OpenAI's automatic prompt caching enabled by default?
questions.description: Use the current OpenAI prompt-caching guide. Enter the minimum number of tokens.

images.alt: Three panels on prompt caching. The first compares two prompt layouts: a cache-hostile one that opens with a request id, so the prefix diverges at the first token, and a cache-friendly one that opens with stable instructions and examples and leaves 410 tokens of shared prefix before the request id and user data. The second lists what a hit is — a byte-identical opening, reported in the usage data, cheaper and faster on eligible input — against what it is not: a semantic match, free output, or learning; with a note that automatic caching starts at 1,024 prompt tokens. The third bills ten requests: one uncached at $0.020, nine cached at $0.018, and ten outputs at $0.080, totalling $0.118.
images.caption: A prefix match stops at the first changed token, so where the edit lands decides how much is reused.

questions.explanation: OpenAI documents a minimum of 1,024 prompt tokens for automatic caching. Repeating a shorter prompt does not make it eligible. This threshold belongs to OpenAI's service and is not a universal transformer rule.
questions.references: [OpenAI API: How prompt caching works](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)

options.text: A cache hit requires a matching prompt prefix; similar meaning is not enough
The response usage data can report how many input tokens were served from cache
Cached-input pricing and retention policies can vary by model or provider
A prompt-cache hit makes all generated output tokens free

questions.explanation: OpenAI caching reuses work for a matching prompt prefix and reports cached input in the usage data. Eligible cached input can cost less and process faster, but generated output is still billed. Prices, write costs, and retention rules can vary by model and service.

questions.title: What is the total token cost for this ten-request workload?
questions.description: Each request has `10,000` input tokens and `1,000` output tokens. The initial request is an uncached miss; the next nine have all input tokens cached. Rates are `$2.00 / 1M` uncached input tokens, `$0.20 / 1M` cached input tokens, and `$8.00 / 1M` output tokens. Ignore all other fees. Enter dollars.

images.alt: Three panels on prompt caching. The first compares two prompt layouts: a cache-hostile one that opens with a request id, so the prefix diverges at the first token, and a cache-friendly one that opens with stable instructions and examples and leaves 410 tokens of shared prefix before the request id and user data. The second lists what a hit is — a byte-identical opening, reported in the usage data, cheaper and faster on eligible input — against what it is not: a semantic match, free output, or learning; with a note that automatic caching starts at 1,024 prompt tokens. The third bills ten requests: one uncached at $0.020, nine cached at $0.018, and ten outputs at $0.080, totalling $0.118.

questions.explanation: Uncached input costs `10,000 / 1,000,000 * $2 = $0.020`. The nine cached requests cost `90,000 / 1,000,000 * $0.20 = $0.018`. All outputs cost `10,000 / 1,000,000 * $8 = $0.080`, giving a total of `$0.118`.
questions.references: [OpenAI API: Prompt caching distinguishes uncached, cached, and output-token accounting](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)

questions.title: Which one-character edit is likely to destroy more prefix-cache reuse?

options.text: Changing a character near the beginning of the reusable prompt
Changing a character after the entire reusable prefix
Both edits must preserve exactly the same cached prefix length
Neither edit matters because caches match prompts by topic

questions.explanation: An exact prefix stops matching at the first changed token. An early edit leaves less shared content before that point, so less work can be reused. A change after the stable section can preserve the earlier cached prefix.

questions.title: What does a prompt-cache hit *not* mean?

images.alt: Three panels on prompt caching. The first compares two prompt layouts: a cache-hostile one that opens with a request id, so the prefix diverges at the first token, and a cache-friendly one that opens with stable instructions and examples and leaves 410 tokens of shared prefix before the request id and user data. The second lists what a hit is — a byte-identical opening, reported in the usage data, cheaper and faster on eligible input — against what it is not: a semantic match, free output, or learning; with a note that automatic caching starts at 1,024 prompt tokens. The third bills ten requests: one uncached at $0.020, nine cached at $0.018, and ten outputs at $0.080, totalling $0.118.
images.caption: A prefix match stops at the first changed token, so where the edit lands decides how much is reused.

options.text: That the model's weights were updated to remember the user permanently
That some repeated input computation may be reused
That eligible cached input may be billed at a different rate
That request latency may decrease

questions.explanation: Prompt caching reuses work for a matching input prefix. It does not fine-tune the model, change its weights, or create permanent personal memory. Cache reuse and model learning are separate mechanisms.

questions.title: Which metric tells you how quickly a streamed response starts?

images.alt: Three panels on streaming. The first traces one response on a seven-second ruler: a 1.0-second time to first token, then 100 inter-token intervals spanning 5.0 seconds, with the arithmetic 100 intervals / 5.0 s = 20 tokens per second. The second lists the events of a stream — a message start, three text deltas that split mid-word and mid-timestamp, a message stop, and an error or refusal event — beside three client rules: assemble the deltas, branch on the event type, and never render a chunk as the finished answer. The third contrasts what streaming moves (perceived wait) with what it leaves alone (billable tokens) and what it complicates (moderation, parsing, rollback).
images.caption: Time to first token and throughput are separate numbers, and neither is a discount.

options.text: Time to first token (TTFT)
Total time until the final token only
The model's knowledge-cutoff date
The number of tokenizer vocabulary entries

questions.explanation: Time to first token measures the wait before the first generated content arrives. Total latency measures the wait for the complete response. Streaming can improve when users first see output even if the final token arrives at nearly the same time.
questions.references:
[OpenAI API: Streaming responses](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/streaming-responses)

[OpenAI API: Latency optimization](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latency-optimization)

questions.title: What is the approximate post-start generation throughput in this trace?
questions.description: The initial token arrives at `t = 1.0 s`, and token number 101 arrives at `t = 6.0 s`. Use the 100 inter-token intervals after the initial token. Enter tokens per second.

images.alt: Three panels on streaming. The first traces one response on a seven-second ruler: a 1.0-second time to first token, then 100 inter-token intervals spanning 5.0 seconds, with the arithmetic 100 intervals / 5.0 s = 20 tokens per second. The second lists the events of a stream — a message start, three text deltas that split mid-word and mid-timestamp, a message stop, and an error or refusal event — beside three client rules: assemble the deltas, branch on the event type, and never render a chunk as the finished answer. The third contrasts what streaming moves (perceived wait) with what it leaves alone (billable tokens) and what it complicates (moderation, parsing, rollback).
images.caption: Time to first token and throughput are separate numbers, and neither is a discount.

questions.explanation: The 100 intervals after the first token take `6.0 - 1.0 = 5.0` seconds. Throughput is `100 / 5.0 = 20` tokens per second. The separate time to first token is still 1 second.

questions.title: Which statements about streaming a text response are correct?

images.alt: Three panels on streaming. The first traces one response on a seven-second ruler: a 1.0-second time to first token, then 100 inter-token intervals spanning 5.0 seconds, with the arithmetic 100 intervals / 5.0 s = 20 tokens per second. The second lists the events of a stream — a message start, three text deltas that split mid-word and mid-timestamp, a message stop, and an error or refusal event — beside three client rules: assemble the deltas, branch on the event type, and never render a chunk as the finished answer. The third contrasts what streaming moves (perceived wait) with what it leaves alone (billable tokens) and what it complicates (moderation, parsing, rollback).
images.caption: Time to first token and throughput are separate numbers, and neither is a discount.

options.text: The client can display or process early chunks before the response is complete
Streaming can reduce perceived waiting even when generation finishes at nearly the same time
Partial output can complicate moderation, parsing, and rollback
Enabling streaming guarantees fewer generated tokens and a lower token bill

questions.explanation: Streaming sends incremental events while generation continues. Users can see or process early output sooner, but the model may still generate and bill the same tokens. Applications also need a plan for moderating, parsing, or withdrawing partial output.
questions.references: [OpenAI API: Streaming responses with server-sent events](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/streaming-responses)

The third contrasts what streaming moves (perceived wait) with what it leaves alone (billable tokens) and what it complicates (moderation, parsing, rollback).

options.text: As incremental pieces to assemble while also handling completion and error events
As independent, complete answers that should overwrite one another
As proof that the final response has already passed every validation step
As model-training updates sent to the browser

questions.explanation: A streamed response is a sequence of events. Text deltas add fragments, while other events can signal completion, refusal, or an error. Clients should follow event types and never assume that a chunk ends at a word, JSON value, or complete answer.

questions.title: Which change usually reduces total generation latency most directly?

images.alt: Three panels on streaming. The first traces one response on a seven-second ruler: a 1.0-second time to first token, then 100 inter-token intervals spanning 5.0 seconds, with the arithmetic 100 intervals / 5.0 s = 20 tokens per second. The second lists the events of a stream — a message start, three text deltas that split mid-word and mid-timestamp, a message stop, and an error or refusal event — beside three client rules: assemble the deltas, branch on the event type, and never render a chunk as the finished answer. The third contrasts what streaming moves (perceived wait) with what it leaves alone (billable tokens) and what it complicates (moderation, parsing, rollback).
images.caption: Time to first token and throughput are separate numbers, and neither is a discount.

options.text: Generate a substantially shorter output that still satisfies the task
Rename a JSON field from `x` to `result` while generating the same number of tokens
Raise temperature solely to make decoding parallel
Move the knowledge cutoff forward in the request body

questions.explanation: Generating output is sequential and often takes most of the request time. OpenAI's guide notes that cutting output length by about half may cut latency by about half, although results vary. Shorter answers can be faster when they still contain everything the task requires.
questions.references: [OpenAI API: Generate fewer tokens to reduce latency](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latency-optimization)

questions.title: If streamed and non-streamed requests generate the same tokens, how does streaming alone affect token cost?

images.alt: Three panels on streaming. The first traces one response on a seven-second ruler: a 1.0-second time to first token, then 100 inter-token intervals spanning 5.0 seconds, with the arithmetic 100 intervals / 5.0 s = 20 tokens per second. The second lists the events of a stream — a message start, three text deltas that split mid-word and mid-timestamp, a message stop, and an error or refusal event — beside three client rules: assemble the deltas, branch on the event type, and never render a chunk as the finished answer. The third contrasts what streaming moves (perceived wait) with what it leaves alone (billable tokens) and what it complicates (moderation, parsing, rollback).
images.caption: Time to first token and throughput are separate numbers, and neither is a discount.

options.text: It does not. Streaming changes delivery timing, not the number of billable tokens
The streamed request's output tokens are always free
The non-streamed request is billed once per HTTP packet
The streamed request automatically uses prompt-cache pricing for output

questions.explanation: Sending the same output in chunks does not change its token count. Streaming changes when content arrives, not how many input or output tokens the model uses. Other provider charges may exist, but streaming alone does not create a token discount.

questions.title: What does strict mode for Structured Outputs add beyond basic JSON mode?

options.text: Conformance to a supported developer-supplied schema as well as syntactically valid JSON
A guarantee that every value in the JSON is factually true
Unlimited output length for JSON responses
Automatic execution of every function named in the schema

questions.explanation: JSON mode aims to produce text that parses as JSON. Strict Structured Outputs also constrain the result to a supported JSON Schema, including required keys and allowed value shapes. A schema-valid value can still be factually wrong.
questions.references: [OpenAI API: Structured Outputs versus JSON mode](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs)

questions.title: What must an application still handle when using strict Structured Outputs?

options.text: A schema-valid value can still be factually wrong
Safety refusals may arrive through a refusal path rather than the requested schema
Reaching the output limit can leave the response incomplete
Every keyword from every JSON Schema draft is necessarily supported

questions.explanation: Constrained decoding controls the shape of a response, not whether its claims are true. OpenAI also documents refusal and incomplete-output cases and supports only part of JSON Schema. Production code should inspect response status, handle refusals, and validate the meaning of parsed values.
questions.references: [OpenAI API: Structured Outputs edge cases and supported schemas](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs)

questions.title: Which schema rules does OpenAI document for strict Structured Outputs?

options.text: Object fields must be listed as required
An optional value can be modeled with a required field whose type also allows `null`
Objects must set `additionalProperties: false`
A root-level `anyOf` is always accepted

questions.explanation: OpenAI requires every object field to be listed as required and every object to set `additionalProperties: false`. A required field can allow `null` when the value is optional in the application. The root schema must be an object and cannot be an `anyOf` union.
questions.references: [OpenAI API: Supported schemas for Structured Outputs](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs#supported-schemas)

questions.title: Why can the first request with a new Structured Outputs schema be slower?

options.text: The service may need to process the schema before constrained generation, and that preprocessing can be reused
The model permanently retrains all of its weights on the schema
JSON requires a slower network protocol than text
The initial response must always contain every possible schema-valid object

questions.explanation: OpenAI notes that a new schema can add latency while the API processes it for constrained generation. Later requests with the same schema can avoid that extra step. This processing does not train the model or change its weights.
questions.references: [OpenAI API: Initial schema-processing latency](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs)

questions.title: What does a model's knowledge cutoff mean?

options.text: The latest date covered by the model's built-in knowledge, as defined by the provider
The date when every fact before it was verified as true
The date after which the model refuses to process user-provided text
The expiration date of the API key

questions.explanation: A knowledge cutoff marks the latest date covered by a model's built-in knowledge, according to the provider. It does not guarantee that every older fact is present or correct. The model can still analyze newer information supplied in the prompt or fetched with tools.
questions.references: [OpenAI API: Model catalog lists knowledge cutoffs](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models)

questions.title: Which statements about knowledge cutoffs are correct?

options.text: Different model versions can have different cutoff dates
A model can reason over post-cutoff material supplied through retrieval or tools
A confident answer about a post-cutoff event is not proof that the model has current knowledge
Every fact before the cutoff is guaranteed to be present and accurate

questions.explanation: Cutoff dates can differ between models and versions. Search tools and retrieved documents can add newer information to a request without changing the model's built-in cutoff. A confident tone is not proof of freshness, so current claims still need dated sources.
questions.references:
[OpenAI API: Models have distinct knowledge-cutoff metadata](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models)

[OpenAI API: Web search supplies up-to-date information](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-web-search)

questions.title: Which practices make answers about fast-changing facts more reliable?

options.text: Retrieve current information from authoritative sources and preserve source timestamps
Record the model ID or snapshot and its documented knowledge cutoff
Evaluate citation support, freshness, and abstention behavior on representative cases
Raise temperature until the answer sounds confident

questions.explanation: Reliable current answers need more than a model's built-in knowledge. Use dated, authoritative sources, record the model version and cutoff, and test whether the application cites or abstains when evidence is weak. Raising temperature adds variation; it does not update the facts.
